Senses.Explanation: Something described this way is perfectly round on every side, with no edge, corner, or seam. The expression occurs 132 times in 81 allowlisted texts. Hongzhi Zhengjue supplies the clearest physical constraint by saying that it is perfectly round and has no edges or corners. Shuzhong Wuyun applies the description to a begging bowl, calling it round and shining before describing where he throws or stores it. Yinyuan Longqi makes the same shape mobile by comparing it to a pearl running on a tray and a tray moving under the pearl; he then calls it perfectly round and lively, emerging and disappearing and opening and folding. In a separate three-part exchange, Yinyuan answers “what is buddha?” with “perfectly round,” “what is the teaching?” with “lively and active,” and “what is the monastic community?” with “freely at ease.” Zen bends a visible round, cornerless form into public answers and paired descriptive formulas, but the headword itself does not name one hidden substance, attainment, or universal abstract meaning.
Senses.Note: Other predicates retain the same rounded form while attaching different claims to it. Qianyan Yuanzhang pairs “perfectly round” with “shining and flashing,” then says “large within large, narrow within narrow.” Hongzhi Zhengjue says that the form is neither the least bit deficient nor the least bit excessive. Chunan Furong Baining Yi also criticizes a fixed reading: he says later people take “the perfectly round and shining one” as the ultimate rule, yet do not know that the Way has no fixed body and that heading toward it goes astray. His warning prevents the dictionary from converting a recurrent description into one universal abstract definition. The adverbial form occurs 15 times in 11 texts, and the exact round-and-shining pairing occurs three times in three texts.

Senses.Explanation: The phrase denotes awakening characterized as sudden rather than staged gradually. Huineng says one's own nature awakens itself, with sudden awakening and sudden refinement and no gradual sequence. An unnamed monk contrasts sudden awakening of principle with gradual removal of affairs and asks Sanzu Chonghui for its principle. A case narrative describes Bao'en Xuance awakening suddenly at the fire-boy answer. Guxue Zhe likewise contrasts principle, which must be awakened to suddenly, with affairs removed gradually. Yongming Yanshou places sudden awakening in a fourfold matrix with gradual awakening and sudden or gradual refinement. Guifeng Zongmi defines turning from ordinary person to sage as sudden awakening. Yulin Tongxiu asks whether an addressee has the capacity for sudden awakening and sudden refinement. These uses distinguish sudden awakening from later refinement without forcing every record into one historical classification.
Senses.Note: Seven exact lexical witnesses across six distinct works cover self-awakening, encounter narration, sudden/gradual contrast, a fourfold matrix, direct definition, and capacity test. The longer Treatise on the Essential Gate of Entering the Way through Sudden Awakening title was excluded under the substring gate and buys no bare-headword depth.

Senses.Explanation: A paired contrast, literally 'sudden and gradual.' The term occurs 275 times in 104 allowed texts. The Platform Record reports that people spoke of Southern Huineng and Northern Shenxiu and therefore made a Southern/Northern division of sudden and gradual. Huineng's recorded correction is explicit: 'The teaching is originally one lineage; people are northern and southern. The teaching is one kind; seeing has slowness and speed. What is called sudden and gradual? The teaching has no sudden and gradual; people are sharp and dull, and therefore it is called sudden and gradual' (法本一宗，人有南北。法即一種，見有遲疾。何名頓漸？法無頓漸，人有利鈍，故名頓漸). Another recension puts it as 'seeing slowly is gradual, seeing quickly is sudden' (‘seeing slowly is gradual; seeing quickly is sudden’), again followed by 'the teaching has no gradual and sudden'. Later texts likewise say that sudden and gradual have no difference (頓漸無殊), or that whichever order is stated—'gradually refining, suddenly understanding' (漸修頓悟) or 'suddenly understanding, gradually refining' (頓悟漸修)—one must finally arrive personally once. The Record of the Source-Mirror enumerates four textual combinations: gradually refining and suddenly understanding, suddenly understanding and gradually refining, gradually refining and gradually understanding, and suddenly understanding and suddenly refining. That list records combinations of words; it does not override the Platform Record's direct correction or establish a hierarchy. The corpus contains five occurrences of 'the teaching has no sudden and gradual' (法無頓漸).
Senses.Note: The Platform Record locates slowness and speed in seeing and sharpness and dullness in people; later texts record the sudden/gradual combinations. In those cited combinations, 'refining' (修) translates the recorded graph literally.
